verdicts.note: Watch-out called the finite disjoint unions of intervals (a,b] an algebra on R; that needs endpoints -inf <= a < b <= inf, since complements are unbounded. Also introduced the notation sigma(E), which later cards use without definition.
Counting measure was used here and in later cards without being defined; added its definition next to the Dirac measure.

Watch-out said restricting test sets 'to measurable sets' gives a useless condition: circular, and wrong for outer measures induced by a premeasure, where testing on the algebra suffices. Kept the correct subsets-of-E point and noted that only test sets of finite outer measure need checking.
Counterexample's 'finite unions of Q intersect (a,b]' is not an algebra on Q unless a and b may be infinite; added the endpoint range.
Used the indicator chi_(0,inf) before indicator notation is introduced (simple-function card); defined it inline.
Same teaching-order issue: chi_[0,inf) used before chi is defined; defined it inline.

Said m* is 'additive only on measurable sets', which is false (m* is additive on non-measurable sets at positive distance, for example); now says countably additive on the measurable sets but not on all of P(R^n).
Key idea said measurability is used 'exactly once' and then named two steps; reworded to the single subtraction in step 1, reused for E^c in step 3.

Finite unions of bounded dyadic boxes do not form an algebra on R^n; now allows infinite endpoints and says countable additivity carries nu = c m to them. Replaced the unclear 'counting measure on a discrete copy of R' with counting measure on the Borel sets of R.
Wrote {0,2}^N, which under the notation sheet (N starts at 0) indexes from 0, while the ternary expansion indexes from k >= 1; now {0,2}^{Z>0}.

Watch-out claimed no translation-invariant extension of m to all subsets of a positive-measure set exists; the argument does not show this and the statement is not well posed. Replaced with the correct point that the proof is non-constructive and rests on the axiom of choice.
The Cantor function is not a taught term and was described only by properties that do not determine it; added its definition on C and on the removed intervals.
Watch-out named the fat Cantor set K_alpha, clashing with the problem's density constant alpha; renamed it K.
Complex-valued measurable functions are used from Egorov's theorem on (and in the integrable-function card) but were never defined; added that f is measurable when Re f and Im f are.
Said the integral of sum a_j chi_{E_j} is sum a_j mu(E_j) for any real a_j, which can be inf - inf; restricted to a_j >= 0 with 0 * inf = 0, matching the integral definition card.
Used f^+ and f^- before they are defined (integrable-function card); defined them inline.

The statement for arbitrary measurable E is correct, but the proof sketch uses Egorov, which needs m(E) < inf. Marked the sketch as the finite-measure case and added the reduction over bounded shells.

Watch-out cited the typewriter sequence to show domination is not necessary, but that sequence is dominated by 1 on [0,1). Replaced with (1/n) chi_[n,n+1] (converges in L^1, no integrable dominator), kept the typewriter sequence for a.e. convergence, and fixed 'the next two cards' (the next card is the proof idea).
Used 'uniformly integrable' six cards before it is defined; reworded the watch-out without the term.
'The failure is not in convergence type', followed by the ways it fails other convergence types, contradicted itself; rewritten to say plainly that the convergence is only pointwise.
Watch-out said 'a bound that grows with t is not enough', which is false (a factor bounded for t near the point is fine). The real requirement is one integrable bound valid for all t near the point.
Answer line credited dominated convergence with finiteness, which comes from the integrable dominator itself; also used the subset sign ⊂, which the notation sheet does not define (now ⊆).

Claimed that on a finite measure space a.e. convergence plus uniform integrability is equivalent to L^1 convergence. False: the typewriter sequence converges in L^1 but nowhere pointwise. Now: L^1 convergence iff convergence in measure plus uniform integrability, with the a.e. version only sufficient.

Step functions took the sup and inf over the open piece, which need not give the Darboux sums; now over the closed piece. Replaced 'Darboux's theorem' (the taught term is the derivative intermediate value theorem) with the mesh-to-zero statement it meant, and defined the oscillation.
The answer to 'when does it make sense' gave only measurability; for signed f the integrals must also exist (f >= 0 or integrable integrands). Added.
Used 'monotone class' without defining it; added the definition inline.
Listed the Lebesgue times counting diagonal among the examples for 'if f is not integrable'; that example has a nonnegative f and fails sigma-finiteness instead. Separated the two failure modes.

Claimed both iterated integrals define measures on B x B, but x -> c(E_x) need not be Borel measurable for Borel E (the projection of a Borel set can be non-Borel). Now contrasts the genuine measure E -> sum_y m(E^y) (value 0 on D) with the Caratheodory-Hahn product (value inf on D).
Ref pointed to Folland ch. 2; the distribution-function formula is in Folland ch. 6 (section on distribution functions). Dropped the unverified Stein-Shakarchi pointer.

Gave the wrong reason why changing f, g on null sets does not change f*g ('(x,y) -> x-y preserves null sets'); the reason is that y -> x-y preserves null sets for each fixed x. Folland ref moved from ch. 2 to ch. 8 (convolutions).
Ref pointed to Folland ch. 2; Minkowski's inequality for integrals is in Folland ch. 6. Dropped the unverified Stein-Shakarchi pointer.

Used 'Banach space' (not taught) and C_c(X) and support without defining them; now an infinite-dimensional normed vector space, with support and C_c(X) defined. Ref moved to Folland ch. 4, where these spaces are defined; Stein-Shakarchi does not treat them.

Claimed every Dirac measure on a topological space is regular; false when points are not closed (Sierpinski space), so now on a Hausdorff space. Also '(next card)' pointed at the Radon card instead of the metric-space regularity card.

'The Riesz representation theorem' clashes with the taught Hilbert-space theorem of that name; clarified it is the one for positive linear functionals on C_c(X). Dropped the Stein-Shakarchi ch. 6 ref, which has no Radon measures.
Refs pointed to Folland ch. 7 (Radon measures) and Stein-Shakarchi ch. 6, neither of which contains the C^1 change of variables theorem; now Folland ch. 2.
Same ref fix as the theorem card; also ⊂ replaced by ⊆ per the notation sheet.
Typed card accepted only 2pi/sqrt(3) and 2pi/sqrt3; added the rationalized forms (2sqrt(3)pi/3 and variants) and (2pi)/sqrt(3), an answerDisplay, and 'exactly' in the prompt.
⊂ replaced by ⊆ per the notation sheet.

Step 2 chose U1 containing E with only mu(U1) < inf, then claimed an open U2 containing U1 minus E with mu(U2) < eps, which is impossible unless mu(U1 minus E) < eps. Now U1 is chosen with mu(U1) < mu(E) + eps first. Refs narrowed to Folland ch. 7.
